item.title: On the First Day of School, a Test for Mamdani’s 2-K Program
item.description:
More than 780,000 public schoolchildren across New York City flooded into classrooms on Thursday morning, bringing a mix of excitement and trepidation as summer break gave way to the first day of school.

The day was especially momentous for the youngest students in the school system’s history: About 2,000 entered the city’s first free child care program for 2-year-olds, the signature education initiative of Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has pledged to create a universal child care system from infancy to kindergarten.

Yet the rollout of the new 2-K program, along with the existing 3-K and pre-K programs, has been hobbled by funding delays and late payments. Lacking city funds, some day care directors have taken out personal loans or asked staff to work without pay. A few centers, including at least one 2-K site, were closed on Thursday, saying that they could not afford to open.

“We have to see the money come in,” said Patricia Chin, who still planned to open her two Brooklyn day care sites offering 2-K on Thursday. She drained her personal savings to pay her center’s expenses, which she said were more than $130,000 a month. “It is bad not knowing, especially for the wages and the rent,” she said.

The debut of 2-K was supposed to be a moment of celebration for Mr. Mamdani and the beginning of financial relief for families with younger children. In New York City, child care is often the largest expense after housing. Private care can cost $20,000 to $50,000 a year in New York.

More than 5,700 families applied for one of the coveted seats in existing child care sites, which are in four largely low-income areas of the city. Mr. Mamdani plans to expand the program with another 10,000 seats next year.

After some child care directors publicly revealed their dire situations, Mr. Mamdani promised to “bring every resource to bear” to resolve the logjam, expedite disbursements and deliver supplies before classes began. Many providers reported progress in recent days, saying their funding requests had been approved, and money — in the form of interest-free bridge loans — had been deposited into their accounts. Still, it arrived too late for some to purchase essential items like furniture.

But with more than 1,100 centers across the city, some directors were still waiting for relief and were without reserves to sustain daily operations.

Mr. Mamdani said on Thursday that his administration had made headway in delivering funds to centers. He said that the city had registered contracts for more than 500 day care centers and had disbursed more than 300 loans, which cover a month’s expenses.

“I am fully confident in our team in continuing that work,” Mr. Mamdani said at a news conference in Manhattan for the first day of school along with Gov. Kathy Hochul and Kamar Samuels, the schools chancellor. “We know that this is going to be a critical part of delivering universal child care, and we are looking forward to that.”

Richard R. Buery Jr., a nonprofit leader who oversaw the creation of the city’s first universal prekindergarten expansion in 2014, said the start of 2-K was exciting and a “really powerful milestone.” He said he was worried about the payment delays, noting that they were longstanding and complicated to fix.

“My concern is 2-K relies so heavily on home care settings,” he said. “As painful as contract delays are, they are actually devastating for home care providers. I know the city recognizes this and is trying to address it.”

Many parents were excited to get a 2-K seat. But some decided not to accept their offers and said they were not fully comfortable with the day cares they were matched with.

Sarah Henderson, a mother in the Inwood neighborhood of Manhattan who was offered a 2-K seat for her daughter, said she was disappointed that her current day care was not included. She had never heard of the local programs, which are mostly home day cares listed under the director’s name, and wasn’t ready to take a leap of faith.

“We’re going to keep her in her current day care,” she said. “Her brother is already there after-school.”

Expanding to younger children could require building trust with families of toddlers who require more support. They are still learning to use the bathroom and taking naps. More staffers are needed for 2-year-olds — one for every six children, compared with one staffer for every 10 3-year-olds, according to city regulations.

The first 2-K students arrived at the Friends of Crown Heights center in Inwood on Thursday morning and said goodbye to their parents with hugs and tears. They had snack time, munching on crackers and sipping apple juice, and gathered on a brightly colored rug to dance to music. Parents were excited and nervous, making last minute diaper changes and asking about school uniforms.

Sepporah Harkless’ daughter Harmony walked in and began to play with toys. Ms. Harkless said that getting a 2-K seat meant that she could return to work at an Amazon warehouse.

Six students showed up on Thursday, though 10 names were on the attendance list and the center had capacity for 12 students. Justin Joseph drove from East Elmhurst in Queens to drop his daughter Leona.

“It’s monumental for us, and it’s great for her — the socialization, the education,” Mr. Joseph said.

In the weeks ahead of the first day of school, day care directors had been stressed about the prospect of starting the school year without money. The providers have complained for years about late reimbursement payments, but few could recall not receiving funds for upfront costs before the first day.

Rachel Surizon, the director of Renanim Preschool in the Bronx, said the center has not received funding for its new 2-K program, and she’s worried about how she’ll pay teachers. She received puzzles for the classroom on Wednesday, and the city has provided some other materials like markers, diapers and wipes.

“Everything is so vague,” Ms. Surizon said. “We don’t have answers.”

Providers traditionally receive early payments under their annual contracts just before school begins to fund initial operating costs. But this year, every contract was extended, which required them to be reviewed again and shared with the Office of the New York City Comptroller to be registered. By September, about 10 percent of the contracts had been registered.

While contracts were being processed, city leaders encouraged providers to apply for bridge loans, but even those have taken weeks or longer to be disbursed. In recent days, directors have been pleading with officials at the city’s Department of Education, which operates the child care program, for the money to be released.

The Mamdani administration said it has moved employees from other departments to speed up the release of payments and registration of contracts. It is also hiring more employees in the Department of Education’s early childhood education division, where the top official resigned last month. A new leader was named on Tuesday, Erica Phillips, who had been the executive director of the National Association for Family Child Care.

Candie Woo, who runs the Little Tulip Daycare Center of Little Neck in Queens, said that when she asked department officials about her $100,000 loan request this week, she was told that if Little Tulip did not open on Thursday, the department would reassign her students to another center, depriving her of all funding.

“We don’t deserve that type of treatment,” said Ms. Woo, who has 48 children at her center and plans to welcome children on Thursday despite the lack of money.

But Anna Marie Alleyne, who runs two centers in Brooklyn that serve 186 children in 3-K and pre-K, said she simply could not afford to open. Despite repeated inquiries, Ms. Alleyne said, she got approval only on Tuesday for a loan at one center and just for expenses from July. Her 52 employees were not paid in August, leading three of them to quit.

“How can I ask staff to come in when they haven’t received a paycheck?” said Ms. Alleyne, whose centers cost nearly $300,000 a month to run. “They are demoralized and broke.”

On Thursday morning, more than 20 workers from several closed centers rallied outside City Hall, having raised money just to cover their travel to the demonstration. Karen Copeland, a 3-K teacher, said that she had stopped payments on her life and car insurance and canceled a vacation to see her daughter in North Carolina.

“I spent my vacation depressed, in bed,” Ms. Copeland said.

Nate Schweber contributed reporting.

item.title: Who Says Reading Is Dead?
item.description:
I hate to go all Andy Rooney, but why do so many people watch stuff with the captions on?

I used to think that if the captions were on when I started streaming a show, it must be a mistake, and I’d irritatedly turn them off. But now it seems that captions-on is the default mode for streamers.

To me, captions have been for the hard of hearing or when the source is in a foreign language. But one survey found that most Americans use captions sometimes or always, and among younger people, 40 percent use them often or always. This includes most people I know.

I have been asking around, and the explanations make some sense. Many say it helps them understand more of the dialogue, especially when the English is a different dialect like Scottish or even just British. But also when it’s just plain American. I used to just take it for granted that you would lose a word here and there, especially in a movie, and especially when first settling into it. After all, we do in real life. But there’s no reason we have to settle for that with TV and movies now that technology allows us to get every word. I used to tell foreigners, including even Brits and Australians, that they might find “The Wire,” with its rapid, overlapping and thick Black English, tough to understand. That was 20 years ago — now they can caption it.

And sure, the captions are useful if you’re watching on your phone in a public place and have the grace and sophistication not to play the audio out loud. I’m also told that captions allow you to engage with your TikTok or show while texting someone — I can’t quite say I get why anyone would want to do this, but I don’t judge! (Usually.)

But really, all of this dances around how often people must be using captions when none of these explanations apply. I have watched a group of tweens savoring “The Simpsons” insisting on having the captions on while focusing on nothing but the show in a cozy room with the volume way up. A “Simpsons” audio track is crystal clear, and no one is mumbling or having baroquely crisscrossing conversations.

Another example — a group of people in late middle age whom I watch old movies with (I, of course, am a mere 39!) includes a Russian couple with fantabulous English. But even people as tippy-top level as them in English can find it hard to hear through the hissy “mud” of the soundtrack of older films. So we put the captions on for them — but this summer, even when they happened not to be with us, everybody (but me) wanted to use the captions anyway.

To wit, captions have become routine, even if studies show that you spend about a quarter of your time reading the captions rather than watching the picture.

I am as surprised by this as I was when cellphones happened and a great many people proceeded to talk on the phone on and off 24/7. Because now they could, of course, but I had no idea people actually wanted to talk that much.

What helped me get closer to an answer was a friend of my tween daughters who said she finds it more stimulating to read rather than to just hear. She said, “I like reading, and with the captions it’s just bam, the words!”

I think it’s a sign of what happens to our sense of language when literacy becomes widespread, as the professor of literature Walter Ong wrote of in his magnificent “Orality and Literacy.”

Literacy, Ong wrote, fashions a sense that written language is “real” language while spoken language is an inexact approximation of it.

In that vein, captions naturally seem like a completion of spoken dialogue, laying out in full what just talking only approximates — “Bam, the words!” In her article for The Atlantic “The End of Reading Is Here,” Rose Horowitch argued that we are becoming a post-literate society. She is dead on in terms of longform prose, but the preference to see Marvel films captioned shows that our brains are still “on writing,” just as one can be on a drug. Literacy transforms how we process language. Once technology allows us to watch speech joined by its written equivalent, we embrace the writing — speech is completed if we see it simultaneously spelled out.

The president’s observation that “most people” don’t know that the word “dumb” ends with a b is relevant here. Of course, almost everybody knows that dumb is spelled with a b, and they did in the Middle Ages as well. So many knew that it screwed up how other words were spelled. If a literate person knew that “dumb” was spelled with a b but the b wasn’t pronounced, then — in worship of writing — you thought “thumb,” “numb” and “limb” must have a silent b at the end as well. That’s most likely why we spell them with a b. Dumb comes from an ancient word with an actual b, but the others should be spelled “thum,” “num" and “lim.” Only “comb" actually had the original b as well.

In a show tune from 1939, Richard Rodgers and Lorenz Hart complained about jazz instrumentalists improvising on the melody — “I Like to Recognize the Tune.” With my similarly retrograde attitude, my song would be “I Like to See the Whole Damn Screen!”

item.title: Apple’s New Foldable iPhone Is Here. How Do We Review It?
item.description:
It doesn’t flip — it folds. That was the buzz when Apple unveiled its new iPhone Duo this week at a media event in Cupertino, Calif. The event gave journalists the opportunity to get a first look at the device, and to briefly try it for themselves ahead of its public release in October.

Brian X. Chen, the lead consumer technology writer for The New York Times; Brenda Stolyar, who covers smartphones for Wirecutter, The Times’s product recommendation site; and Caitlin McGarry, who edits Wirecutter tech coverage, were there to see the device — and its faint crease — themselves. They explained their processes for testing new tech gadgets, and what goes into a review. This conversation has been edited and condensed.

You don’t have access to the iPhone Duo yet. But Apple hosted a press event that gave reporters a peek at how it works. Can you describe what these types of events are like, and what you can glean from them?

BRIAN X. CHEN: Steve Jobs is widely credited for pioneering the product unveiling event, which has been a form of marketing for tech companies showing off new inventions. Lots of companies, including Samsung, Google and Meta, now emulate it. In general, members of the press get invitations to an event where tech executives show off a product; typically we have hands-on time to try the product before it becomes available to the rest of the world. It’s a small window that gives us a glimpse into whether a new technology will become a trend or be a fad.

CAITLIN McGARRY: We also usually get to chat with employees at the companies who have worked on the products, and ask them questions about decisions or features that are confusing or unclear. In the worst-case scenarios at these launch events, the products are behind glass or are running a demo version of the software (or a looping video) that doesn’t replicate the real-world experience of using it. With the iPhone Duo, we were able to try the actual device for about 45 minutes.

Brian, you write The Times’s Tech Fix column, about consumer technology. Caitlin and Brenda, you work for Wirecutter, The Times’s product recommendation site. How do your goals differ?

BRIAN: I tend to stray away from a traditional review format, which is usually an evaluation of a product’s main features (like battery life, screen brightness and camera quality). Instead, I try to think big-picture about the themes of a new technology and whether or not it solves real-world problems. I reviewed the most recent Google Pixel 11 phone, for example, and that device featured new A.I. software that ordered groceries, hailed cars and booked restaurant tables for the user. I asked: Do people really want A.I. that uses their phones for them? I focused on that theme because I was trying to assess whether so-called agentic A.I. is really going to drive the future of personal computing — or if some of these new tools are just gimmicks.

CAITLIN: People come to Wirecutter for recommendations, so our goal is to evaluate what products are like to actually live with. Our readers are curious about the latest technology, but they’re more interested in buying the best possible thing that will last the longest time — and doesn’t cost a fortune. We come up with a list of criteria for evaluating product categories and then aim to test every worthwhile product to figure out which one is the best for most people and often which is best for a particular user or situation.

Apple and other tech companies are protective of their products before they hit the market. What does access look like? Do we keep the products we review?

BRIAN: It’s no secret that some tech companies may prioritize giving early access to writers who they believe will give them favorable coverage. With some companies whose products I’ve reviewed favorably (because I thought the product was simply good), it’s not difficult to continue to get access. But with others whose products I’ve reviewed unfavorably, I’ve been denied access. My goal is to serve the reader and tell them whether or not a piece of technology is worth their consideration, so if a company denies me access, I simply buy the product and test it. If a company provides access, I test a loaner and return it when I’m done. With iPhones, I usually ship them back to Apple within a month after publication.

CAITLIN: Like Brian, journalists at Wirecutter review products regardless of whether a company provides us access to them. If they don’t, we buy them. If they do, we usually get them before they hit stores and have some time to use them in the real world before we review them.

We re-evaluate devices over time and aim to comprehensively compare devices against one another to determine which is best, so our testing period is fairly lengthy compared to other outlets. We send review units back when we finish testing, and we donate devices we no longer need to test, according to Wirecutter’s ethics policy.

What are your editorial processes for tech reviews?

BRIAN: Whenever I test a product, I put myself in the shoes of someone who is not working in Silicon Valley — my relatives, my nanny, my kid’s preschool teacher — and I try to think from a down-to-earth perspective about what matters to people and whether or not this new gadget is going to be useful for them. Most people just want to feed their families, take care of their health, shoot nice pictures and get their work done.

CAITLIN: Wirecutter has a whole team of consumer technology reporters, and our review process varies depending on what we’re testing. When we review devices like routers, laptops and monitors, we put them through an intensive benchmarking process to capture objective measurements. And then we actually live with those products to see what features improve your quality of life and which ones are simply annoying (the classic flaw but not deal breaker).

Wirecutter’s journalists have full editorial control over what to test and which products to recommend. We have no insight into decisions about things like affiliate links, which are the responsibility of our commerce department. Wirecutter’s newsroom operates independently of the revenue side.

BRENDA STOLYAR: Like Caitlin said, we live with these products. For example, with smartphones, I use each review unit as my primary device, implementing the same habits and usage that I would with my standard device — using it for social media and transportation apps, making phone calls and sending texts, shooting and editing photos, and more. This gives me the most realistic insight into its hardware (based on how comfortable it is to use and travel with), as well as how it performs and how long the battery lasts.

How long will you use a product like an iPhone before publishing a review?

BRIAN: Usually about a week. In the past, companies gave us two weeks before lifting embargoes for when we were allowed to publish reviews, but these embargoes have gotten shorter and shorter over the years, which is not ideal. But there are also so many products out there and companies competing for your attention, so I get it.

CAITLIN: Our review timeline is similar, but in many cases we update reviews again and again with long-term test notes after publishing our initial review. If we run into issues with a device and need more time with it, we’ll skip the embargo so we can figure out if the issue is serious and widespread or if we got a lemon (which occasionally happens).

How many brands of phones do we test and evaluate in a typical year?

BRIAN: I don’t review very many because I like to focus on a few each year that represent new trends, such as A.I. or foldable screens. But when I do a review, I also tend to request loaners of a few competing devices so I have comparisons.

BRENDA: Each year, we review phones from all the major phone manufacturers, including Apple, Samsung, Google and Motorola. But we also test phones from smaller brands doing interesting things. Each brand also offers different categories of devices, including flagship, budget, foldable and midrange phones. These releases are staggered throughout the year, so we’ll review a variety of models from each brand.

CAITLIN: We test cheap phones under $200, and $2,000 foldable phones. We have recommendations for folks who don’t want to spend a lot of money and for early adopters who want the latest and greatest.

What else do readers need to know about the way we vet a flashy new product?

BRIAN: Because The Times is independent and we’re primarily supported by subscribers, we’re here to serve you — not to hype up every shiny new thing. That’s largely why you’ll see real-talk advice from me, like how instead of buying this year’s new phone, you’d probably be happy buying a refurbished version of last year’s phone and save a good buck, especially with the A.I.-induced chip shortage driving the price of everything up.
